latin.239: Noli mihi objicere peccatum esse interdum poenam peccati. Primum enim non est poena quatenus peccatum, nisi velis duas species mali oppositas inter se confundere, sublato inter malum poenae & culpae discrimine. Privatio autem justitiae in nobis, qua talis, formaliter peccatum est; repugnat enim legi. Deinde id non est accipiendum de poena proprie & stricte accepta, qualem lex comminatur & justitia necessario exigit ut sibi satisfiat. Quis enim credat justitiam exigere ut justitia violetur? satisfieri justitiae eo quo justitia laeditur? solvi poenae debitum eo, quo debitum illud augetur? Adjungi praecepto, ne violetur, comminationem poenae sitae in violatione praecepti? pergo igitur.
latin.240: Quarta ratio, poena proprie dicta sive mors quam lex comminabatur sequi debuit quaestionem ac judicium Dei de violatione illius legis. Sed privatio justitiae sive mors spiritualis quaestionem ac judicium Dei de violatione legis sequuta non est, sed antecessit: non fuit igitur poena proprie dicta, sive mors quam lex comminabatur.
latin.241: Quinta denique ratio, (caeteras enim differre, & in alium locum conferre satius erit.) Si lex Adamo mortem sitam in privatione justitiae comminabatur, Adamus (ut tu asseris) prout Deus minatus fuerat, Mortuus est. Id autem mihi falsum videtur. Nam primo, Tu, opinor, fateris Adamo condonatum fuisse primum illud peccatum, numerando alioquin inter damnatos: non igitur, prout Deus minatus fuerat, mortuus est. Pugnant enim haec duo, condonari peccatum & puniri secundum legem. Deinde, Tu per mortem denunciatam comminatione tam mortem corporis & aeternam intelligis, quam spiritualem illam. Pertinebat igitur aeque ad veritatem comminationis & justitiam, ut, quo die legem violavit, eodem tam corporea & aeterna morte, quam spirituali moreretur. Tamen eodem die neutram passus est, aeternam autem nunquam subiit, aut subibit. Cur non potuit Adamo mortis spiritualis aeque ac aeternae poena condonari? aut saltem differri?
latin.242: His accedat Scripturae Testimonium: colligens enim summam annorum vitae Adami Gen. v. vers. 5. non contenta iis verbis, quibus in similibus computationibus solis usa est constantissime, interferuit haec duo, וַיְחִי, proculdubio nec frustra, nec temere: quo tamen pertineant non video, nisi ut innuatur, Adamum, ut ferebat divina comminatio, non fuisse mortuum, sed vixisse; quod aliunde quam a Dei gratia, & Domini nostri Jesu Christi satisfactione proficisci non potuit. Hoc ipsum etiam ex eo potest intelligi, quod sententia Adamo lata in paradiso non fuit definitiva, sed quasi interlocutoria, dans spatium homini ad resipiscendum, dilato post mortem extremo judicio, ac interim conditionem hominis definiens, mediam quodammodo inter damnatum & absolutum. Hinc factum est, ut, neque Deus hominem pronunciaverit maledictum, quemadmodum serpentem, sed terram duntaxat. Et quamvis morti corporeae eum addixerit sententia, tamen circumlocutione usus sit, nec mortem eam appellare voluerit, ne videretur pertinere ad Comminationis legis executionem. Fuit igitur judicium illud, non extremum (hoc enim Adamo post mortem subeundum fuit juxta illud Apostoli, statutum est hominibus ut semel moriantur, postea vero judicium Heb. 9.) sed praemissum extremo in aliud tempus dilato. Vide sis Thesium mearum de lapsu Adami ultimam.
latin.243:
Si igitur Deus pro summa sua misericordia & sapientia comminationis illius executionem distulit, ac suspendit ex alio judicio post separationem animae a corpore futuro, fatendum est Adamum non fuisse, prout ferebat legis comminatio, Mortuum. Itaque comminationem illam de spirituali morte posita in privatione justitiae non esse intelligendam, quam ego arbitror ipsa morte aeterna deterius malum esse.

GAR. Additur & tertia ratio. Si lex Adamo mortem sitam in privatione justitiae comminabatur, Adamus, prout Deus comminatus erat, mortuus fuerit, quod falsum; cum inter damnatos non sit computandus. Item, cum mors illa aeternam, corporalem, & spiritualem complectatur, qui nunquam sensit aeternam, nec statim sensit temporalem, quomodo spiritualem, nempe privationem justitiae, statim incurrisset? Respond. 1. Qui mortuus est morte sita in privatione justitiae, si in ea perseveret, usque ad finem, inter damnatos computandus est. At non ita factum Adamo, qui fide in semen benedictum ex illa morte spirituali in vitam spiritualem excitatus est, ut fit omnibus electis, quos mortuos in peccatis placet Deo vivificare in Christo, Ephes. 2.
latin.244: PLAC. Cur hanc rationem, cum sit quinta, tertiam vocet, causam nullam video, nisi quia, cum duas praeterierit, secundam & quartam, videri tamen noluit ullam praetermisisse. Quatuor etiam rationibus minorem hujus argumenti quinti confirmaveram: ex quibus solas priores duas sibi objicit, sed ita contractas, praesertim primam, ut vix eam agnoscam. Adhibet autem responsiones duas, quibus argumentum firmare potius videtur, quam infirmare. Priore rationem reddit, cur Adamus non fuerit damnatus. Concedit igitur, (quae minoris argumenti mei confirmatio erat) eum non fuisse damnatum. Sic enim se habebat argumentum meum; Si lex Adamo mortem sitam in privatione justitiae comminabatur, Adamus secundum legis comminationem punitus est. Atqui Adamus secundum legis comminationem punitus non est. Ergo Lex non comminabatur Adamo mortem sitam in privatione justitiae. Quid respondet Vir Doctus ad Majorem? Num eam negat? Num distinguit? Num ei limitationem adhibet? Nihil prorsus respondet. Eam igitur concedit. Ita videtur. Potest tamen limitari: cum enim praeter illam privationem, etiam corporis & aeternam mortem lex minaretur, Adamus secundum legis comminationem partim punitus fuisset, partim non fuisset: Punitus fuisset illa privatione seu morte spirituali, non fuisset punitus morte corporis & aeterna. Sed haec limitatio argumento nihil nocet. Punitus enim saltem fuisset poena aliqua proprie dicta, seu judiciaria quam Lex comminabatur, & quidem poena maxima. Id autem est falsum. Fecit enim ei Deus gratiam peccati. Non punitur autem cui peccatum remittitur, cui peccatum non imputatur, qui justificatus est a peccato. Nam si partim puniretur, partim non puniretur, etiam ei partim peccatum remitteretur, partim non remitteretur, & partim justificaretur, partim non justificaretur; imperfectaque esset justificatio, id quod Evangelicorum nemo dixerit. Cum tale sit argumentum meum, vides, lector, hanc priorem Viri Docti responsionem illius neque majorem, neque minorem labefactare. Pergat igitur.

pass_a.239: Do not object to me that sin is sometimes the punishment of sin. For first it is not punishment insofar as it is sin, unless you wish to confuse two opposite species of evil with each other, the distinction between the evil of punishment and of fault having been removed. But privation of justice in us, as such, is formally sin; for it is repugnant to the law. Next that is not to be taken of punishment properly and strictly accepted, such as the law threatens and justice necessarily demands that satisfaction be made to itself. For who would believe that justice demands that justice be violated? that justice be satisfied by that by which justice is injured? that the debt of punishment be paid by that by which that debt is increased? that there be joined to the precept, lest it be violated, a threat of punishment situated in the violation of the precept? I proceed therefore.
pass_a.240: Fourth reason: punishment properly so called, or the death which the law was threatening, ought to have followed God's inquiry and judgment concerning the violation of that law. But privation of justice, or spiritual death, did not follow God's inquiry and judgment concerning the violation of the law, but preceded it: it was not therefore punishment properly so called, or the death which the law was threatening.
pass_a.241: Fifth reason finally (for it will be better to put off the rest and transfer them to another place). If the law was threatening Adam with death situated in privation of justice, Adam (as you assert) died just as God had threatened. But that seems false to me. For first, you, I suppose, confess that that first sin was forgiven to Adam, otherwise numbering him among the damned: he did not therefore die just as God had threatened. For these two fight each other, that sin be forgiven and that one be punished according to the law. Next, by the death denounced in the threat you understand both the death of the body and the eternal, as well as that spiritual one. It belonged therefore equally to the truth of the threat and to justice that, on the day he violated the law, on the same he should die both by bodily and eternal death and by spiritual. Yet on the same day he suffered neither, and the eternal he never underwent, nor will undergo. Why could not the punishment of spiritual death equally with eternal be forgiven to Adam? or at least deferred?
pass_a.242: To these let the testimony of Scripture be added: for collecting the sum of the years of Adam's life, Gen. 5:5, not content with those words which in like reckonings it has most constantly used alone, it inserted these two, וַיְחִי, doubtless neither in vain nor rashly: yet to what they pertain I do not see, except that it be hinted that Adam, as the divine threat carried, had not died but had lived; which could not proceed from elsewhere than from the grace of God and the satisfaction of our Lord Jesus Christ. This very thing can also be understood from this, that the sentence passed on Adam in paradise was not definitive, but as it were interlocutory, giving space to the man for repentance, the extreme judgment after death having been deferred, and meanwhile defining the man's condition as somehow middle between the damned and the absolved. Hence it came about that God neither pronounced the man cursed, as he did the serpent, but only the earth. And although by the sentence he sentenced him to bodily death, yet he used a circumlocution and was unwilling to call it death, lest it seem to pertain to the execution of the Law's Threat. That judgment therefore was not the extreme (for this Adam had to undergo after death according to that of the Apostle, it is appointed for men to die once, and after this the judgment, Heb. 9) but one sent ahead of the extreme deferred to another time. See if you will the last of my Theses on the fall of Adam.
pass_a.243: If therefore God out of his supreme mercy and wisdom deferred the execution of that threat, and suspended it from another judgment future after the separation of soul from body, it must be confessed that Adam was not, as the law's threat carried, Dead. And so that threat concerning spiritual death placed in privation of justice is not to be understood [as I take the threat], which I judge to be a worse evil than eternal death itself. GAR. There is added also a third reason. If the law was threatening Adam with death situated in privation of justice, Adam, just as God had threatened, would have died, which is false; since he is not to be numbered among the damned. Likewise, since that death embraces the eternal, the bodily, and the spiritual, he who never felt the eternal, nor at once felt the temporal, how would he at once have incurred the spiritual, namely privation of justice? Reply 1. He who has died the death situated in privation of justice, if he perseveres in it unto the end, is to be numbered among the damned. But it was not so done to Adam, who by faith in the blessed seed was raised from that spiritual death into spiritual life, as it is with all the elect, whom dead in sins it please God to make alive in Christ, Eph. 2.
pass_a.244: PLAC. Why he calls this reason third, when it is fifth, I see no cause, except that, having passed over two, the second and the fourth, he yet did not wish to seem to have omitted any. I had also confirmed the minor of this fifth argument with four reasons: of which he objects to himself only the prior two, but so contracted, especially the first, that I scarcely recognize it. But he brings two replies by which he seems rather to strengthen the argument than to weaken it. By the prior he gives the reason why Adam was not damned. He therefore concedes (which was the confirmation of the minor of my argument) that he was not damned. For so my argument stood; If the law was threatening Adam with death situated in privation of justice, Adam was punished according to the law's threat. But Adam was not punished according to the law's threat. Therefore the Law was not threatening Adam with death situated in privation of justice. What does the Learned Man reply to the Major? Does he deny it? Does he distinguish? Does he apply a limitation to it? He replies nothing at all. He therefore concedes it. So it seems. Yet it can be limited: for since besides that privation the law was also threatening bodily and eternal death, Adam according to the law's threat would have been partly punished, partly not: he would have been punished by that privation or spiritual death, would not have been punished by bodily and eternal death. But this limitation does the argument no harm. For he would at least have been punished by some punishment properly so called, or judicial, which the Law was threatening, and indeed the greatest punishment. But that is false. For God granted him grace of the sin. But he is not punished to whom sin is remitted, to whom sin is not imputed, who has been justified from sin. For if he were partly punished, partly not, also to him sin would partly be remitted, partly not, and he would partly be justified, partly not; and justification would be imperfect, which no one of the Evangelicals would say. Since such is my argument, you see, reader, that this prior reply of the Learned Man shakes neither its major nor its minor. Let him proceed therefore.

239: Do not tell me that sin is sometimes the punishment of sin. First, sin as sin is not punishment—unless you mean to smash together two opposite kinds of evil and erase the line between penalty and guilt. Privation of righteousness in us, as such, is formally sin; it clashes with the law.

Second, that claim is not about punishment properly and strictly so called—the kind the law threatens and justice must have satisfied. Who believes justice demands that justice be broken? that justice is paid by wounding justice? that the penalty-debt is settled by making the debt larger? that a threat whose penalty is the very breach of the precept should be tacked onto the precept "do not break it"? I go on.
240: Fourth proof. Proper punishment—the death the law named—has to come after God has examined and judged the breach. Loss of righteousness, spiritual death, did not wait for that examination and judgment; it arrived first. Therefore it was neither proper punishment nor the death the law was threatening.
241: Fifth proof (I put the rest off for another place). If the law threatened Adam with death as privation of righteousness, then—on your view—Adam died just as God had threatened. That looks false to me. First, you yourself, I take it, grant that Adam's first sin was forgiven; otherwise he would be counted among the damned. So he did not die just as God had threatened. Forgiveness of sin and punishment according to the law cannot both stand.

Second, by the death named in the threat you mean bodily death and eternal death as well as spiritual. Truth and justice in the threat would then require that on the very day he broke the law he die bodily, eternally, and spiritually. Yet that day he suffered neither bodily nor eternal death, and eternal death he never underwent and never will. Why could spiritual death's penalty not be forgiven Adam as eternal death's was—or at least deferred?
242: Add Scripture's witness. When Genesis 5:5 totals Adam's years, it is not content with the words it always uses alone in like reckonings; it inserts these two, וַיְחִי—surely neither for nothing nor by chance. I see no point for them except to hint that Adam, as the divine threat would have it, had not died but had lived—and that life could come only from God's grace and our Lord Jesus Christ's satisfaction.

The same follows from the paradise sentence: it was not definitive but, as it were, interlocutory—giving the man room to repent, deferring the last judgment until after death, and meanwhile setting his state somehow between the damned and the acquitted. Hence God did not call the man cursed as he did the serpent, but only the ground. And though the sentence bound him to bodily death, it spoke by circumlocution and would not name it "death," lest it look like executing the Law's threat. So that judgment was not the last (Adam must face that after death, per the Apostle: it is appointed for men to die once, and after that judgment—Heb. 9) but a preliminary to the last, deferred to another time. See the last of my Theses on Adam's fall.
243: If then God in supreme mercy and wisdom deferred executing that threat, hanging it on another judgment after soul and body part, we must grant Adam was not Dead as the law's threat required. So the threat of spiritual death as privation of righteousness is not to be read as I take that threat—which I judge a worse evil than eternal death itself.

Garissoles. A "third" reason is added. If the law threatened Adam with death as privation of righteousness, he would have died as God threatened—which is false, since he is not to be counted among the damned. And since that death covers eternal, bodily, and spiritual: he who never felt eternal death, nor at once felt temporal, how did he at once incur spiritual death—privation of righteousness? Reply 1. Whoever dies the death of privation of righteousness and stays in it to the end is counted among the damned. Not so Adam: by faith in the blessed seed he was raised from that spiritual death into spiritual life, as with all the elect whom God is pleased to make alive in Christ when dead in sins (Eph. 2).
244: Placeus. Why call this the third reason when it is the fifth? I see no cause except that, having skipped the second and fourth, he still did not want to seem to have skipped any. I had backed this fifth argument's minor with four reasons; he takes up only the first two, so compressed—especially the first—that I scarcely know them. His two replies seem to shore the argument up more than tear it down.

The first explains why Adam was not damned—and so grants what confirmed my minor: he was not damned. My argument ran: If the law threatened Adam with death as privation of righteousness, Adam was punished as the law threatened. But he was not. Therefore the Law did not threaten him with that death. What does Garissoles say to the major? Deny? Distinguish? Limit? Nothing at all—so he concedes it.

One might limit: besides that privation the law also threatened bodily and eternal death, so Adam would have been partly punished (by spiritual death) and partly not (by bodily and eternal). The limit does not hurt the argument. He would still have been hit by some punishment properly so called—judicial, and the greatest—which the Law threatened. That is false. God granted him grace for the sin. The one whose sin is remitted, not imputed, who is justified from sin, is not punished. Partial punishment would mean partial remission and partial justification—an imperfect justification no evangelical would own. So, reader, this first reply shakes neither major nor minor. Let him go on.
